mainTopic: How a small estate (נכסים מועטין) is divided between daughters' sustenance and sons' inheritance: רבא's rule, what happens if the estate's value changes, and whether a widow's sustenance counts in the calculation.
overview: The גמרא rejects a view that would hand the daughters the whole estate. It adopts רבא's rule instead: the daughters' sustenance is set aside until they become adults, and the sons get the rest. It then states that if a large estate shrinks, the sons keep it, since they already acquired it. Next it asks what happens when a small estate grows. It answers from רבי יוחנן's ruling that orphans' sale of a small estate is valid, which shows the heirs still own it. After that, רבי ירמיה asks רבי אבהו a chain of questions about which claims are subtracted when deciding whether an estate is 'small'. The chain runs from the widow's sustenance, to support pledged to a stepdaughter, to a debt owed to a creditor. Some report that he asked the chain in reverse order, starting with the creditor, and that version continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Should the daughters really take everything?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the previous suggestion, which would let the daughters take the whole estate.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall the daughters take all of it?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pushing back hard against the view it just heard. That view would give the daughters the entire estate, even the part they don't need for their food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Daughters are entitled to מזונות (sustenance), not to the inheritance itself. A rule that hands them the whole estate, including the extra beyond their needs, gives them more than their right. That doesn't make sense, so the view is rejected.

phrases.english: Shall the daughters take all of it?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the view stated just before this section on the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: The prior suggestion that the daughters receive the whole estate.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The daughters' right is only to sustenance. Giving them the surplus too gives them more than their right.

steps.title: רבא: Set aside the daughters' food, the rest goes to the sons
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that the court sets aside enough sustenance for the daughters until they reach adulthood, and the sons get whatever is left.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: We set aside sustenance for the daughters until they reach adulthood, and the rest goes to the sons.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the corrected rule. The daughters get exactly what they need to live on until they grow up, and the sons inherit the rest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fixes the problem from step 1. The daughters' claim is limited to their actual sustenance until בגרות, and the sons, who are the real heirs, take any surplus. Each side gets what it is entitled to.

keyTerms.meaning: we take out, set aside (from the estate)

steps.whatToRemember: Daughters get only their sustenance until adulthood. Any extra goes to the sons.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
We set aside sustenance for the daughters
phrases.notes: The court is the one doing this, taking it out of the estate.

phrases.english: until they reach adulthood,
and the rest goes to the sons.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected view with a new rule.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacement of the rejected position with a new rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The daughters might take the entire estate.
steps.terutzMaskana: The daughters take only sustenance until בגרות, and the surplus goes to the sons.

steps.title: Obvious case: a large estate that shrank stays with the heirs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא states it is obvious that if the estate was large and then shrank, the sons already acquired it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious: if the property was large and became small, the heirs already acquired it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states an easy case first. This sets up the harder question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the father died, the estate was נכסים מרובין, so the sons inherited it right away. Losing value later doesn't take away what they already acquired. They keep it and must still support the daughters from it.

phrases.english: It is obvious:
if the property was large and became small,
the heirs already acquired it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about changes in the estate's value, starting with the easy case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If an estate was large at the time of death and later shrank, the sons already own it.

steps.title: What if a small estate grows?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether, when a small estate increases in value, the increase belongs to the sons or whether the sons were fully removed from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it was small and became large, what is the law? Does it stay in the heirs' possession, so it grew in their possession? Or perhaps the heirs are completely removed from it?
steps.whatsHappening: Now comes the hard case. The estate started small, so the daughters' food came first, but then it grew. Who gets the increase?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to see it. Maybe the sons still own a small estate and the court only holds it for the daughters, so any growth is theirs. Or maybe a small estate leaves the sons' ownership completely, so the growth goes along with the daughters' sustenance.

keyTerms.meaning: small (an estate too small for both)

phrases.english: If it was small and became large, what is the law?
Does it stand in the heirs' possession,
so it increased in value in the heirs' possession;
or perhaps,
the heirs are completely removed from here?
phrases.notes: 'From here' means from this property, so the sons would have no hold on it at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the obvious case to the case that is in doubt.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a small estate stays in the sons' ownership, so that its increase in value belongs to them.

steps.title: Proof: orphans' sale of a small estate is valid
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings רבי יוחנן's ruling that if orphans sold land from a small estate before the court acted, the sale is valid. This shows the sons still own a small estate.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי אסי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Orphans who went ahead and sold from a small estate, what they sold is sold.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 4 with a proof. The sons sold land from a small estate, and the sale holds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You can only sell something you own. If the sons' sale of a small estate is valid, they must still own it. So any growth in value happens in their ownership and belongs to them.
steps.whatToRemember: A small estate still belongs to the sons. Their sale of it is valid, so its increase in value is theirs.
steps.confusionAlert: Valid does not mean allowed. The sons should not have sold, but once they did, the sale stands.

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: as Rabbi Asi said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
Orphans who went ahead and sold
phrases.notes: They sold before the court set the property aside for the daughters' food.

phrases.english: from a small estate —
what they sold is sold.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the question of step 4 by bringing a source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A small estate remains the sons' property, so its increase in value belongs to them.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the heirs keep ownership of a small estate.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אסי in the name of רבי יוחנן: the orphans' sale of a small estate is valid.

steps.title: Does the widow's sustenance make the estate count as smaller?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks רבי אבהו whether the widow's right to sustenance is subtracted when deciding whether the estate is small or large.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה was sitting before רבי אבהו and asked him: His widow, does she reduce the estate? Do we say that since she has a right to sustenance, she reduces it? Or perhaps, since if she remarried she would not have it, now too she does not have it?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. When we measure whether an estate is 'small' or 'large', do we first subtract what the widow needs for her food?
steps.deeperAnalysis: One side says she has a real right to מזונות right now, so her share should be taken off and the estate counts as smaller. The other side says her right can disappear if she remarries, so it is not fixed and should not count. The גמרא does not answer directly. Instead, steps 7 and 8 build further questions on a possible answer.

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya was sitting before Rabbi Abbahu
and he asked him:
His widow, does she reduce the estate?
phrases.notes: He means: does her food count against the estate, so it is judged 'small'?

phrases.english: Do we say:
since she has a right to sustenance, she reduces it;
or perhaps,
since if she would remarry she would not have it,
now too she does not have it?

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ וְקָא בָּעֵי מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about how to measure whether an estate is small or large.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the widow's right to sustenance is subtracted when deciding if the estate is מועטין or מרובין.

steps.title: Does a stepdaughter's support reduce the estate?
steps.stepSummary: Suppose the widow's sustenance is not subtracted, since she loses it if she remarries. Then what about support the father pledged to his wife's daughter? That pledge continues even after she marries, but it ends if she dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that since the widow would lose her support by remarrying, she counts as having no claim even now, then what about the man's stepdaughter? Does her support reduce the estate? Maybe yes, since she keeps it even when she marries. Or maybe no, since she would lose it if she died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא assumes an answer to the widow question from step 6 and uses it to ask a new, harder question about a stepdaughter's support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The widow's claim might be ignored because it can easily end through remarriage. The stepdaughter's claim is stronger because marriage does not end it. Still, it ends if she dies, so the question is whether a claim that can end in any way counts as not yet real.

keyTerms.meaning: If you will say. It opens a follow-up question that builds on a possible answer to the previous one.
His wife's daughter, meaning his stepdaughter from her earlier marriage
She reduces the estate. Her claim is subtracted when deciding if the estate is small.

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether the stepdaughter gets paid. She does. The question is only whether her claim is subtracted when deciding whether the estate counts as 'small' for the daughters' sustenance rule.

phrases.english: If you say:
since if she remarries, she does not have it,
now too she is treated as not having it;
his wife's daughter: does she reduce the estate?
phrases.notes: This is a man who promised to support his wife's daughter for some years. That promise binds his estate even after he dies.

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן: כֵּיוָן דְּכִי מִנַּסְבָא נָמֵי אִית לַהּ – וּמְמַעֲטָא;
phrases.english: Do we say: since even when she marries she still has it, she reduces the estate;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֵּיוָן דְּאִילּוּ מֵתָה לֵית לַהּ – וְלָא מְמַעֲטָא?
phrases.english: or perhaps, since if she dies she does not have it, she does not reduce the estate?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם תִּמְצָא לוֹמַר: כֵּיוָן דְּאִילּוּ מִנַּסְבָא לֵית לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a follow-up question on a possible answer to the widow question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a stepdaughter's support, which survives her marriage but ends at her death, is subtracted when measuring the estate

steps.title: Does a debt owed to a creditor reduce the estate?
steps.stepSummary: Suppose the stepdaughter's support is not subtracted, since it ends if she dies. Then what about a creditor? His claim survives even his own death, but the money has not been collected yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the stepdaughter's support does not reduce the estate because she would lose it by dying, then what about a creditor? Maybe his debt reduces the estate, since even if he dies his heirs still collect. Or maybe it does not, since the debt has not been collected yet.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא climbs one more level. It asks about a creditor, whose claim is the strongest of all because even death does not end it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The widow can lose her claim by remarrying, and the stepdaughter can lose hers by dying. The creditor never loses his claim, because his heirs inherit it. The only reason not to subtract it is that the money is still sitting in the estate and has not actually been collected.

keyTerms.meaning: A creditor, someone the deceased owed money to
It still needs collection. The money has not yet been taken.
Or perhaps. It introduces the second side of a question.

steps.whyThisMatters: The chain shows a ladder of ever-stronger claims: one ended by remarriage, one ended only by death, and one not even ended by death. Each level asks whether the claim is 'real' enough to subtract.

phrases.english: And if you say:

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דְּאִילּוּ מֵתָה לֵית לַהּ – וְלָא מְמַעֲטָא;
phrases.english: since if she dies she does not have it, she does not reduce the estate;
a creditor: does he reduce the estate?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן: כֵּיוָן דְּכִי מָיֵית נָמֵי אִית לֵיהּ, מְמַעֵט;
phrases.english: Do we say: since even when he dies he still has it, he reduces the estate;
phrases.notes: 'He' here is the creditor: even after he dies, his heirs still collect the debt.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֵּיוָן דִּמְחַסְּרִי גּוּבְיָינָא, לָא מְמַעֵט?
phrases.english: or perhaps, since it still needs to be collected, he does not reduce the estate?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּמְצָא לוֹמַר: כֵּיוָן דְּאִילּוּ מֵתָה לֵית לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a further follow-up question on a possible answer to the stepdaughter question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an uncollected debt, which survives even the creditor's death, is subtracted when measuring the estate

steps.title: Another version: the questions asked in reverse order
steps.stepSummary: Some report that רבי ירמיה asked the same questions in the opposite order, starting with the creditor.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say he asked it the other way around: a creditor, does he reduce the estate?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second report of the same questions, this time in reverse order. It opens with the creditor, and this sets up the rest of the reversed chain that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, each 'if you say' assumed the weaker claim does not reduce the estate, then asked about a stronger one (widow, then stepdaughter, then creditor). Starting with the creditor flips this. The follow-ups would assume the stronger claim does reduce the estate and then ask about weaker ones.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say he asked it, meaning another version of the question
In the other direction, meaning in reverse order

phrases.english: And some say he asked it the other way around:
a creditor: does he reduce the estate?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternate version of the same chain of questions in reverse order
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a creditor's claim reduces the estate, asked as the first link of a reversed chain
